body.heading: The same letters, a different story
paragraphs: An anagram rearranges every letter of a word or phrase to make a new one. Listen becomes silent, triangle becomes integral, and dormitory, with a bit of cheek, becomes dirty room. Nothing is added and nothing is taken away — only the order changes.
The best anagrams feel like a joke the letters were keeping. “The eyes” turns into “they see”, and “astronomer” becomes “moon starer”, which is almost a job description.

body.heading: A famous arithmetic trick
paragraphs: Here is a gem to test carefully: “eleven plus two” is an anagram of “twelve plus one”. Count the letters of each side and you will find thirteen on both — and, delightfully, both sums equal thirteen too.

Writers have played this game for centuries. In the 1600s, King Louis XIII of France employed a royal anagrammatist whose job was to rearrange the king's name into flattering phrases for court entertainment.

body.heading: Try it: anagram your name
paragraphs: Write your name in capital letters, then cut the letters out or use letter tiles so you can slide them around. Look for small words first — at, in, art, ten — then see what is left over. Vowels are precious: a name with two or three is far more generous.
Set a house rule before you start: every letter must be used exactly once, and ordinary dictionary words only. Then challenge a friend to beat your best find from the same set of letters.

takeaway: Every word is a crowd of other words waiting to be let out — shuffle the letters and see who appears.
